name: Voyager — Checkout availability
description:
The proportion of five-minute slices over a 30-day rolling window in which every run of the [Voyager] Checkout funnel browser synthetic passed, against a 99.0% objective (01-PRD.md § 6.2).

This is the only SLO in Voyager measured from outside the system. The other two are built from the application's own telemetry, which means they cannot see a failure that stops requests arriving at all — a broken TLS certificate, a Caddy misconfiguration, a JavaScript bundle that will not parse. A browser test walking the real funnel does see those, and that is the whole reason this objective exists.

Why a time-slice rather than a monitor-based SLO: a time-slice SLO treats missing data as uptime, which is the correct behaviour for a synthetic that runs on a fixed schedule rather than continuously. A gap in test runs is not evidence that checkout was down.

The threshold is 1 with a >= comparator, so a slice counts as good only if the pass ratio is 1 — every run in that five minutes succeeded. With the test on a five-minute interval that is one run per slice, so a single failure costs one slice, which is 0.0116% of a 30-day window. The budget tolerates roughly 86 failed runs per month before the objective is missed.

One constant here could not be verified from Datadog's public documentation: the `status` tag value that marks a passing run of `synthetics.test_runs`. It is written as `status:0`. If that is wrong, the numerator will be empty and the SLO will read 0% — a loud, immediately obvious failure rather than a permanently green one, which is the safer way to be wrong. Confirm it against a real test run before trusting the number, and see datadog/README.md.
